segments.en: High above you in a palm forest, a seed is growing that can weigh as much as a small child. It's the coco de mer, the largest seed of any plant, and it grows naturally in only two places on Earth, both of them here in Seychelles.
That forest is the Vallée de Mai on the island of Praslin, cool, shady and full of rustling giant leaves. If you're lucky, you'll spot the rare black parrot, darting between the palms.

Seychelles is a scattering of about a hundred and fifteen islands in the Indian Ocean, far off the coast of East Africa. Some are tall and made of ancient granite, covered in green hills, while others are low coral islands barely rising above the waves.
On La Digue, people get around by bicycle, and the beaches are famous for their enormous smooth granite boulders, pink and grey, standing in shallow turquoise water like sleeping giants.

Nobody lived on these islands until the seventeen hundreds. Then came French settlers and enslaved Africans, later British rule, and people from India, China and beyond. Seychelles became independent in nineteen seventy-six.

All those roots grew into one Creole culture. The everyday language is Seychellois Creole, known as Kreol Seselwa, based on French, and English and French are official languages too. A friendly bonzour will open many doors.
Far to the southwest lies Aldabra, a huge coral atoll that is home to tens of thousands of giant tortoises. You'll meet them on the main islands too, sometimes munching grass in people's gardens.
Food here is full of the sea and spice. Try a fish curry made with coconut milk, octopus curry, grilled red snapper, and chutneys made from green papaya or mango, all served with rice.

Listen for the moutya, a slow, powerful dance rooted in the days of slavery, when people gathered by firelight to drum and sing. Today it's a proud symbol of Seychellois heritage, alongside the lively sega.

The capital, Victoria, on the main island of Mahé, is one of the smallest capital cities in the world. At its centre stands a little silver clock tower, and nearby the market sells fish, spices and tropical fruit.
The ocean is at the heart of everything, with coral reefs full of colourful fish, green sea turtles nesting on quiet beaches, and whale sharks gliding past in certain seasons.
Mersi, thank you, for your visit. Sail south across the Indian Ocean, and the island of Mauritius, another Creole-speaking home, is waiting to welcome you.
